description: Overproduction, speculation and the panic of Black Thursday — how the 1920s bubble burst in 1929.
content_html:
The Seeds of Collapse: Overproduction and Underconsumption

Even as the 1920s boom appeared to be at its height, deep structural weaknesses were developing beneath the surface. The most fundamental was the gap between what American factories could produce and what consumers could afford to buy. Overproduction had been building throughout the decade. Factories, driven by mass production techniques, could turn out goods at a rate that outstripped real demand. Once hire purchase credit was exhausted and storage warehouses filled up, factories began cutting production — and with cuts in production came lay-offs and falling wages.

This problem was made worse by the unequal distribution of wealth. The top 5 per cent of Americans received roughly one-third of all personal income in 1929, while tens of millions of farmers, unskilled workers and Black Americans had little disposable income. When factories produced consumer goods in vast quantities, there was a finite number of people who could afford to buy them, even on credit. Falling agricultural incomes meant that the rural half of the population was a weak consumer base throughout the decade.

Key Fact

By the late 1920s, American manufacturers were producing more goods than consumers could buy. Unsold goods piled up in warehouses. Companies began cutting output and laying off workers, reducing consumer purchasing power further — a downward spiral that made the economy increasingly fragile before the Wall Street Crash of October 1929.

Speculation and the Stock Market Bubble

While the productive economy was showing signs of strain, the stock market was booming. Throughout the 1920s, rising share prices attracted millions of ordinary Americans into the stock market for the first time. Between 1920 and 1929, share prices on the New York Stock Exchange roughly tripled. The belief that share prices would always rise encouraged reckless speculation.

The most dangerous practice was buying on the margin. Investors typically paid only 10 per cent of a share’s price upfront, borrowing the rest from their stockbroker. This worked brilliantly when prices rose — investors could sell at a profit and repay the loan. But if prices fell, the broker could demand immediate repayment of the loan (a “margin call”), forcing investors to sell shares at a loss. The entire system depended on prices continuing to rise.

The Wall Street Crash was not the first speculative collapse of the decade. Between 1924 and 1926, a land speculation boom in Florida drew hundreds of thousands of investors. Property prices in Miami doubled, then doubled again, as speculators bought and resold plots of land at rising prices without any intention of building on them. The boom collapsed in 1926, partly because of a devastating hurricane that killed approximately 400 people. Millions of investors lost their money. The Florida collapse was a warning of what happened when asset prices lost touch with underlying value — a warning that went unheeded on Wall Street.

Key Fact

Black Thursday fell on 24 October 1929. Around 12.9 million shares were sold in a single day as investors panicked. On “Black Tuesday” five days later, on 29 October 1929, over 16 million shares were traded, and the market collapsed catastrophically. Billions of dollars of paper wealth were wiped out within days.

The Crash: Panic Selling and Market Collapse

By September 1929, share prices had begun to slide. Nervous investors started selling. As prices fell, margin calls went out to investors who had borrowed to buy shares; to pay their debts, they sold more shares, pushing prices down further. The Wall Street Crash was self-reinforcing — falling prices caused selling which caused further price falls.

On 24 October 1929 — Black Thursday — approximately 12.9 million shares changed hands as panic spread. Leading bankers temporarily steadied prices by purchasing shares, but the recovery was brief. On 29 October — Black Tuesday — more than 16 million shares were traded in a single day, and prices collapsed. By mid-November 1929, share prices had fallen by approximately 40 per cent from their September peak. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, which had reached 381 points in September 1929, eventually bottomed out at 41 points in July 1932 — a fall of nearly 90 per cent from its peak.

The Crash did not cause the Great Depression on its own — it triggered a crisis whose roots lay in overproduction, agricultural decline, unequal wealth distribution and weak banking regulation. As share prices collapsed, banks that had lent money for stock speculation faced ruin; many called in loans to businesses, which then cut production and laid off workers. Consumer spending collapsed as millions became unemployed. By 1933, approximately 13 million Americans — around 25 per cent of the workforce — were unemployed, and thousands of banks had failed.

The international consequences were equally severe. American banks recalled loans to European countries, pushing Germany and other fragile economies into depression. World trade collapsed as countries raised tariffs against each other. The “Roaring Twenties” ended not with a gradual fading but with a catastrophic collapse that transformed the economic and political landscape of the Western world for the next decade.
exam_tip_html: For questions about the causes of the Wall Street Crash, always distinguish between underlying structural weaknesses (overproduction, agricultural decline, unequal wealth, buying on the margin) and the immediate trigger (panic selling from September to October 1929). Examiners look for understanding of how multiple causes connected. For significance questions, remember to address both the immediate consequences (billions lost in days, bank failures) and longer-term significance (triggering the Great Depression, transforming American politics under Roosevelt). Do not simply describe the events of Black Thursday — explain why they happened and what they meant.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Wall Street Crash was rooted in structural weaknesses: overproduction outstripping consumer demand, unequal wealth distribution, and reckless stock speculation financed by buying on the margin. The Florida land bubble of 1925–1926 was an earlier warning that went unheeded.
  • Black Thursday (24 October 1929) saw approximately 12.9 million shares sold in panic; Black Tuesday (29 October) brought over 16 million shares traded and full market collapse. By mid-November, share prices had fallen roughly 40 per cent from their September peak.
  • The Crash triggered the Great Depression. Banks failed, businesses cut production, and by 1933 approximately 25 per cent of the American workforce was unemployed. The international consequences included bank loan recalls to Europe and the collapse of world trade.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the practice of buying shares on the margin.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for identifying a feature; one mark for supporting detail.
Example: Investors typically paid only 10 per cent of a share's price upfront [1], borrowing the remaining 90 per cent from their stockbroker with the shares as security — if prices fell, the broker could demand immediate repayment, forcing panic selling. [1]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Wall Street Crash of October 1929.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per feature.
Feature 1: Black Thursday (24 October 1929) saw approximately 12.9 million shares sold in panic [1], the biggest single-day trading volume the exchange had seen and the beginning of the market collapse. [1]
Feature 2: By mid-November 1929, share prices had fallen approximately 40 per cent from their September peak [1]; the Dow Jones Index eventually fell nearly 90 per cent from its 1929 high of 381 to a low of 41 in July 1932. [1]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why overproduction was a major cause of the Wall Street Crash.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear causal chain from overproduction through declining profits to loss of investor confidence, with precise evidence.
Secure: Valid explanation with supporting detail.
Developing: Names overproduction but mechanism poorly explained.
Emerging: Simple point.
Overproduction: factories produced more than consumers could buy — unsold stock piled up; companies cut output and laid off workers; reduced wages reduced consumer demand further; declining corporate profits spooked investors and contributed to the selling that triggered the Crash.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Wall Street Crash for ordinary Americans.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Traces a consequence with precise evidence and a clear link from Crash to outcome.
Secure: Valid consequence with supporting detail.
Developing: Names a consequence without full explanation.
Emerging: Simple point.
Valid consequences: bank failures as banks that had lent for speculation collapsed; mass unemployment (approximately 25% by 1933); falling wages and consumer spending; evictions from homes as mortgages were called in; the Great Depression's human cost.

practice_questions.text:
How significant was buying on the margin in causing the Wall Street Crash of 1929?
Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Addresses significance with both evidence and analysis of how buying on margin connected to the Crash's mechanism.
Secure: Explains significance with relevant detail.
Developing: Some explanation; may not fully develop the mechanism.
Emerging: Simple points.
Significance: enabled mass participation in stock market with borrowed money; made investors vulnerable to any price fall (margin calls forced selling); self-reinforcing downward spiral once selling began; banks exposed through their lending; billions in paper wealth wiped out within days. Limits: overproduction and structural weaknesses in the economy were the deeper cause; the Crash would not have been as severe without those foundations.

practice_questions.text:
'The Wall Street Crash was mainly caused by speculation rather than economic weaknesses.'
How far do you agree with this interpretation? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Agrees and disagrees with specific evidence for both positions, reaching a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Points for and against; judgement present.
Developing: Unbalanced or underdeveloped.
Emerging: Simple agreement.
Agreement: buying on margin made crash catastrophic — 10% down meant small falls triggered mass selling; millions of ordinary Americans speculating with borrowed money; Florida land bubble showed same speculative pattern earlier.
Disagreement: overproduction made corporate profits unsustainable; agricultural decline removed rural consumers; unequal wealth distribution limited real consumer demand; weak banking regulation; these structural factors meant a crash was likely even without reckless speculation.
Judgement: speculation was the trigger but structural economic weaknesses were the underlying cause — without those, the damage of speculation would have been far smaller.

knowledge_checks.q: What name is given to Thursday, 24 October 1929, when approximately 12.9 million shares were sold in panic on the New York Stock Exchange?
What does 'buying on the margin' mean?
options: Buying shares only from American companies
Paying the full price for shares upfront
Borrowing most of the cost of shares from a broker, paying only a small percentage upfront
Selling shares before they reach their maximum value

knowledge_checks.q: The situation in which factories produce more goods than consumers are able to purchase is called _____.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average reached a peak of 381 points in September 1929 before eventually collapsing to _____ points in July 1932.
Match each term to its description:
right: Buying assets to profit from rising prices, not from their genuine long-term value
24 October 1929, when panic selling began on the New York Stock Exchange
Producing more goods than consumers can afford to buy

flashcard_questions.q: What was overproduction, and why did it weaken the 1920s boom?
flashcard_questions.a: Factories made more goods than consumers could buy — unsold stock piled up, companies cut output and laid off workers.

flashcard_questions.q: What was buying on the margin?
flashcard_questions.a: Borrowing around 90% of the cost of shares from a broker, paying only 10% upfront.

flashcard_questions.q: When did the Florida land speculation bubble collapse?
When did Black Thursday occur, and how many shares were traded?
When did Black Tuesday occur, and how many shares were traded?
By approximately how much had share prices fallen from their September 1929 peak by mid-November 1929?
What was the Dow Jones Industrial Average at its peak in September 1929, and at its low in July 1932?
flashcard_questions.a: 381 points in September 1929; 41 points in July 1932.

flashcard_questions.q: Approximately what percentage of the American workforce was unemployed by 1933?
flashcard_questions.a: Around 25 per cent — approximately 13 million people.

flashcard_questions.q: How did the Wall Street Crash affect European economies?
flashcard_questions.a: American banks recalled loans to Europe, pushing fragile economies like Germany into depression.

flashcard_questions.q: What is meant by a 'margin call'?
flashcard_questions.a: A demand from a stockbroker for immediate repayment of a loan used to buy shares, triggered when prices fell.

glossary_terms.definition: A situation in which factories produce more goods than consumers are able or willing to purchase, leading to falling prices, reduced profits and eventual production cuts.
The practice of buying shares, land or other assets with the expectation of making a quick profit from rising prices, rather than from the asset's genuine long-term value.
Borrowing money from a stockbroker to buy shares, paying only a small percentage (typically 10%) of the cost upfront, with the shares themselves as security for the loan.
Thursday, 24 October 1929, when approximately 12.9 million shares were traded on the New York Stock Exchange as investors panicked and began selling, marking the start of the Wall Street Crash.
The collapse of share prices on the New York Stock Exchange beginning in late October 1929, which triggered the Great Depression.
A situation in which factories produce more goods than consumers are able or willing to purchase, leading to falling prices, reduced profits and eventual production cuts.
